text: — Dravichka, gentlemen, tells it so well that after him it is hard for me to satisfy you with any story. And to tell you the truth, I also know some things about Bay Ganyo — said Vasil. — From Moscow, from Petersburg!
— Start sooner, stop beating around the bush! — replied Dravichkata.
— The word “usukval” does not seem extraordinarily poetic to me — Mato joked.
— Be quiet, gentlemen. Vasile! Come on, little dove, begin!

— On the way to Petersburg — began Vasil — we stopped at the station in Vilno. We were traveling as companions, two of us — Bay Ganyo and I. We went into the buffet. Bay Ganyo wanted me to treat him, since along the way I had been smoking his tobacco. I ordered beer and a snack. The buffet keeper listened to our conversation, recognized, it seems, that I was Bulgarian, and asked us in Russian: — Excuse me, gentlemen, I think you are Bulgarians?
We answered him in the affirmative.
— Don’t you know Mr. Dimitrov, the student?
— I don’t know him; do you know him, Bay Ganyo!
— Dimitrova? Wait... aha! I remember. Dimitrov, I know him, I know him. A very open guy, I know him, of course!
— Can’t you tell me where he is now? — asked the innkeeper.
— He is now in Constantinople — replied Bay Ganyo, — in a week he will be getting married there. He’s struck it lucky!
— Wha-at! — shouted the innkeeper as if thunderstruck. — Get ma-rr-ied? Why, he was married here, gentlemen!...
— Indeed. Look, ha, ha, ha! — laughed heartily Bay Ganyo. The innkeeper looked at him in astonishment.
— You don’t know him — continued Bay Ganyo, turning to me — he’s a terribly sharp lad, that Dimitrov...

The innkeeper told us the following: “One day, gentlemen, Mr. Dimitrov arrived by train with a deaf-mute boy of 13 or 14 years old. I had known Dimitrov a year earlier; he had lived in our town, fell in love with a girl, they got married, and went off to Moscow or to Petersburg—I do not know. When he came this year with the deaf-mute boy, he told me that this boy had a brother in your country, in Bulgaria, a clerk or an officer—I do not remember—who was to send him one hundred francs every month so that he could live in one of the deaf-mute institutions in Petersburg. Since Mr. Dimitrov was leaving for some other city—at least that is what he told me—he asked me to take the boy into my home, feed him, and look after him until his arrival. He assured me that he would return in about ten days. I agreed, took in the unfortunate child, and cared for him as if he were my own. Ten days passed, then a month, then two; no word came from Dimitrov. I wanted to learn something from the child—it was deaf and mute, poor thing, and could not tell me anything. Then I saw that the child had become sad. I wrote to Petersburg, to Moscow—no one replied. In the third month, gentlemen, the boy disappeared. We asked, searched, reported it to the police, sent telegrams in several directions—nothing, the poor child was lost. What became of that child, I still do not know. Let Mr. Dimitrov bear the sin of it; I shall bear a loss of 100 rubles... And you say that he was to be married next Sunday? My God, how is such a thing possible? For God’s sake, gentlemen, report this to your superiors, warn that unfortunate girl whom he is going to marry...”

I promised the innkeeper that as soon as I reached Petersburg, I would inform a gentleman who, I was sure, would immediately telegraph to the Exarchate. I settled my bill. We got on the train and set off for Petersburg.
— You really had to вмешаться — said to me reproachfully Bay Ganyo, — how do you know what sort of woman his local wife is.

We were traveling in third class. Bay Ganyo occupied two seats and lay down to doze. At the next station, several more passengers got into our carriage, and the extra seats had to be given up, but Bay Ganyo is no fool — he pretends to be asleep and snores, snores away. A giant German peasant, with a bag in his hand, came up to Bay Ganyo and began to wake him, gently pushing at his boots. Bay Ganyo hides himself and keeps letting out hrr... puff... hrr... puff... and, covering his face from the German, winks at me, as if to say, “Look how clever I am.” “No, get up!” shouted the German and began to poke my companion rather noticeably. Hrrr... puff!... “Well, don’t pretend, devil!” growled the German, and with one sweep knocked Bay Ganyo’s legs out from under him, toppled him over onto his saddlebags, and sat down with us. Bay Ganyo pretends to be startled, rubbed his eyes, and immediately, as if nothing had happened, took out his snuffbox and offered it open to the German: — Bulgarian tobacco!
— Ah, so you are Bulgarians! Very pleased to meet you — said the German good-naturedly and began rolling himself a cigarette. — You’re going to Petersburg. I am too. Together, then.

As soon as we arrived in Petersburg, I hastened to fulfill my promise to the innkeeper in Vilno. I met with my acquaintance and told him about Dimitrova’s conduct. He immediately telegraphed to Constantinople and managed to stop the impending wedding. In turn, he told me the continuation of the story of the deaf-mute boy. When and how he was persuaded to flee from Vilno is not known, but one day he arrived in Petersburg and there, for a long time, he was the victim of the most base exploitation on the part of Dimitrova, who not only pocketed the sums sent by the brother of the unfortunate boy, but also forced the poor child to go from door to door to all the more influential people and well-known philanthropists in Petersburg to beg for money. And not only in Petersburg, but he often sent him as far as Kronstadt, to the famous saint of the common people, John of Kronstadt...
I, having almost no means of subsistence, was forced to live in Deshovkata, a refuge for extremely poor students. Bay Ganyo insisted most energetically on coming to Deshovkata too.
— Hey, come on, Bay Ganyo, this place is only for students.
— What of it, if it’s for students? — old Ganyo kept trying to persuade me. — Aren’t students people like me? What’s the worst that can happen if they take in a Bulgarian after all?
— But you are a rich man, Bay Ganyo, you can pay at the hotel.

— What a simple fellow you are — Bay Ganyo would chide me. — I thought you were smarter. Hey, Bulgarian, why should we give our money to the Muscovites? If you get hold of a profit, hold it with both hands, eh! How are they to know what my situation is?
— It can’t be done, Bay Ganyo, the poor students will protest, they’ll be angry with me, and they might kick me out of the dormitory.

— Stubborn Bulgarian head! — continued Bay Ganyo. — Why, don’t you have a mouth? Isn’t your wits sharp enough to tell them that I am your brother, that I am a man fallen on hard times; well, it would be enough to say that I am Bulgarian, you know what fools the Russians are!...
— No, no, I can’t! — I cried out resolutely and headed toward Deshovka.

— Hey! You think you’ll get rid of me that easily! Just wait! You haven’t seen anything yet! — grumbles Bay Ganyo and walks after me. — Bulgarian! And this was supposed to be a Bulgarian! Not a shred of patriotism for five cents!... Wait, man, don’t hurry so much, I can’t catch up with you, my saddlebags are heavy! Wait, Bulgarian!...

At that moment we were, it seemed, presenting a rather curious sight, because the people passing along the sidewalks turned around and looked at us attentively. Bay Ganyo, ten paces behind me, with the saddle-bags slung over the stick he carried on his shoulder, and his little rug thrown over the other arm, which he kept lifting now and then to wipe his sweaty forehead. His kalpak was barely holding on to the crown of his head. Bay Ganyo strides along after me and grumbles: “Wait, man of God, at least take the rug, you’re tearing my arm off... You think you can shake me off! You don’t know what a flower old Bay Ganyo is!...” I step as though in bowls and keep thinking how I am going to appear with Bay Ganyo in Deshovka and how I will justify this arbitrary act. I must lie! And yet I see that to get rid of him is impossible! At last, since the matter is only for a few days, I resigned myself to the situation against my will. And Bay Ganyo keeps walking after me, walking, and grumbling all the while, but he has already dropped the swaggering tone and begun in a plaintive voice: “Now listen, Bay Vasile, wait a little, please, Bay Vasile, we are Bulgarians after all...”

And imagine, gentlemen, at that moment I felt sorry for Bay Ganyo! Believe me! I was aware that his conduct was outrageous, that he was a disgusting miser, an egoist, a sly trickster, a hypocritical exploiter, a boor and a lout to the marrow of his bones... but I felt sorry for him: in the subtle vibrations of the tone with which he uttered the last words, my ear caught a tender note that had been hidden, and is hidden, in Bay Ganyo’s heart, but rarely — God, how rarely! — appears... I do not know, it may seem funny to you, unnatural, but I will tell you, gentlemen, that at that moment I looked at Bay Ganyo differently; as if someone had suggested to me: “Do not despise this simple, sly, miserly wretch; he is the offspring of a coarse environment, he is the victim of coarse educators; the evil does not lie in him himself, but in the influence of his surroundings. Bay Ganyo is active, sensible, receptive — above all receptive! Place him under the influence of a good guide, and you will see what feats he is capable of. So far Bay Ganyo has shown only his animal energy, but in him there lies a great reserve of potential spiritual force, waiting only for a moral impulse to turn into living force...”

We arrived in Deshovkata. Most of the students had not yet returned from vacation, so there were quite a few empty places. My bed had been saved by the faithful comrade Kocho, an Albanian, a pauper in the highest degree, who received from the Slavic Society three rubles a month for tea and sugar; he had entered the university, studied there for two years, but, having convinced himself that it was not the work for him, left it and enrolled in the seminary. Good was this Kocho; he would give his head for a friend, but heaven forbid you should irritate him — in an instant all his Arnaut passions would flare up, and he would turn pale, turn green, his eyes would fill with blood, a whole beast!... When Bay Ganya and I entered the room, we found Kocho in a horizontal position on the bed: on that bed it was hard at first glance to tell what was a pillow, what was a mattress, what was a blanket... Kocho sprang from his cot with the lightness of a panther, embraced me, kissed me, introduced himself to Bay Ganya, and, cheerful, laughing from ear to ear with joy, rearranged us to sit, one on the bed, another on a trunk, apologizing for the little disorder in the room. Then he opened the door and let out an Arnaut cry: “Vanka, put the samovar on, my dear!” — “What do you need a samovar for when there’s no tea or sugar!” — replied the dear fellow from the end of the corridor. Kocho seized his head with both hands, crossed the room, grabbed his hat, and, without hearing our pleas for him to stay, that we would buy tea and sugar, rushed out, shouted “right away,” and disappeared... Bay Ganya and I waited half an hour, waited a whole hour — Kocho did not return. Something must have happened to him.

In order not to waste the fine day, I suggested to Bay Ganyo that we go out for a walk. “But wait, let’s wait a bit, the man will treat us to tea,” objected Bay Ganyo; he cannot let a profit slip by, no matter where it appears. But still I insisted on my own. Bay Ganyo stuffed the muskalis into his sash, and we went out. As we were approaching Anichkin Bridge, we heard from afar a savage cry, mixed with the most desperate curses and abuse; we came out onto the bridge and what did we see!... Kocho, raging like a tiger, had his iron fingers dug into the neck of an unknown gentleman, whose hat was rolling on the stones, had bent his head down and was trying to throw him off the bridge. The victim was making every effort to free himself, but it was not so easy to break away from the hands of the crazed Arnaut. “Charlatan! — Kocho roared. — Scoundrel! Villain! You spy, not I, you spy, son of a bitch! I’ll kill you, vile creature!” I rushed to separate them. Bay Ganyo shouted after me: “Leave them, man, why do you need trouble on your head, let them smash each other’s heads; leave them, they’ll drag you around as a witness through the precincts.” I did not heed Bay Ganyo’s advice and headed toward the Arnaut, who did not stop tearing his throat and spewing the most disgraceful epithets at his victim, whom he had already dragged to the edge of the bridge, and, it seemed to me, one more moment — and the unknown man would fly headfirst into the clear waters of the Fontanka. “Charlatan! Scoundrel!” Kocho roared, and dug his bony fingers even more fiercely into his opponent’s thick neck.

When I was already a few steps away from them, the victim, startled by the impending doom, made a desperate movement, tore himself from the Albanian’s hands, snatched up his instantly dirtied hat, and took off running. “Stop, charlatan! Dirty Russian scoundrel!” Kocho grabbed a stone and hurled it after him. The stranger ran up to a tram, jumped inside, and disappeared... But the Arnaut did not calm down: “I’ll kill you, vile charlatan!” — he kept growling, pointing his fist into the space where his enemy had vanished. I called Kocho by name, he turned around and did not recognize me!... There was something beastly in his gaze, his eyes were shining, his face had turned green and dark, his teeth were chattering as in the highest fever, his lips were convulsively trembling and letting out a dull growl. “W... w... b... r... r... Sharrll... Suk... k... p... scoundrel... m... m... m... Charlatan!” — he shouted once more, turning threateningly toward the invisible enemy. “Kocho, little dove, what happened to you, who is this gentleman?” — I asked with friendly sympathy. He fixed his eyes on me and looked at me stupidly and maliciously and still did not recognize me!... “I’ll kill you, vile creature! I’ll show you who the spy is!” — Kocho growled and threatened the passing tram, as if his enemy were sitting in every tram.

“Kocho, please, I beg you, tell me what has happened to you,” I implored my friend, maddened with rage. “Who was that gentleman?” Kocho looked at me once more and shouted: “That is the greatest scoundrel! Do you understand? The grea-test scoun-drel!” — and again he turned away his eyes, and again he set about hurling curses. I began to suspect that my friend was the victim of some villainy devised by his enemy, but what exactly it was, I could not figure out and would not have been able to figure out. What Kocho told me was so vile that it could not even be a matter for conjecture.

Here is what Kocho told us after he came to his senses a little:

“Imagine, gentlemen, when I left Deshovka, I went to the Slavic Society to collect my scholarship, so that I could buy tea and sugar to treat you. You know, Vasile, little dove, what kind of scholarship I receive! Three rubles a month! Three miserable rubles! And imagine, a scoundrel was found who envied me and coveted this wealth of mine. And who? Your compatriot! I congratulate you!... I will knock out the teeth of that charlatan!... Imagine, gentlemen, I go in to the cashier, ask him to give me the three rubles, and he turns to me in an angry tone and says:

— How are you not ashamed, young man, you are a student and you are engaged in such vile deeds!...

— What ‘vile deeds’! — I cried, startled.

— We have information — he continued — that you are a spy for the Bulgarian government.

— What?! I, a spy!

— Yes, we have definite information. Your scholarship has been taken away and given to Mr. Aslanov’s brother.

— For God’s sake, who gave you this information? — I begged through the tears that were choking me with anger.

— Mr. Aslanov himself — he replied calmly.

— ‘A-ah! Bessa-ta-bessa’ — I shouted like a madman and flew out into the street to Anichkin Bridge... you already know!...

My God! Gentlemen, can you imagine anything more despicable!... Charlatan! I... I... I said ‘bessa!’ and I will not forget it!...”

We somehow calmed Kocho down and went with him into a tavern to drink tea. Here we lingered quite a long time, absorbed in the Albanian’s tales of Aslanov’s humiliating escapades. Even Bay Ganyo did not venture to shout his “bravo!” or “ashkolsun!”, but, on the contrary, from time to time clicked his tongue, shook his head in amazement, and said: “Well, I’ll be damned, that man was a complete donkey!” We left the tavern and set off along “Nevsky Prospect.” A mixed crowd from all parts of the world filled the sidewalks of the glittering street; we could barely weave our way among the passersby. Along the street moved, in two rows, every kind of carriage imaginable. One more splendid shop after another lured the eyes of the crowd. Bay Ganyo deigned to express the opinion that “after all, Petersburg is not entirely a bad place”... For a whole hour we pushed our way through the crowd until we reached the Neva. As soon as we came out onto the quieter “English Embankment,” we had not taken even ten steps when Kocho jerked my sleeve in alarm and cried in a choked voice: — There he is!
— Who?
— The charlatan!
— Which charlatan?

— The greatest! Stop! Let’s hide so he doesn’t notice us! — he muttered and dragged us by the sleeves behind the columns of a gate. Bay Ganyo poked his nose out from behind the column and looked in the direction indicated by Kocha.
— Who do you see? — asks Kocho.
— I see a man — whispers Bay Ganyo mysteriously. — Hey, Vasile, look, this man looks very much like our Dondukov-Korsakov.
— He is the same — Kocho replies, — who else do you see?

— I see two more people kneeling before Dondukova, look at that! Th... th... th... th... they’re kissing his boots, crying, begging him for something, beating their chests, look! Th... th... th... th... he wants to shake them off, but they won’t let him go — one on this side, others on that, clutching his legs...
— Look closely, can’t you recognize any of them? — dictated the Albanian.

— I can’t, how am I supposed to recognize them, they’re constantly banging their heads against his boots... Ha, wait — said Bay Ganyo, — wait!... I recognized him! Well, he... it’s true! Well, he’s the one, the one you were going to throw off the bridge... it’s him!
— He is the same... the scoundrel! You are now witnesses to one of his miserable comedies! — growled the Arnaut through clenched teeth. — Come on now, let us slip back into “Nevsky Prospect.”
— Wait, let’s see the end of the scene — I said.

— It’s not necessary — said Kocho firmly, — the ending is known: they’ll hold him by the legs and cry until he gives them a few rubles or some recommendation to another victim, or some intercession... These scoundrels are capable of disgracing the name of an entire nation...
— Well, I’ll be damned! That fellow was a complete donkey — cried Bay Ganyo and clicked his tongue.
— Well, why did you stop, Vasile, keep going! — one of the group called out.
— Tell me about the story with Ermolova...
— Leave it, I’m disgusted — said Vasil.
— Or for Princess Belozerskaya...
— Leave me alone, I can’t take it anymore!
— Well, do you know the story of Bay Ganyo with the tripe soup? — another one chimes in.
— Well, do you know anything about his shaved mustache...

— Enough, gentlemen! Bay Ganyo’s stories never end. Come on, let’s start the second part of the evening already. Marcus Aurelius, sing something, little dove! Or you, Kalina-Malina, sing something!... Come on: “Za-pre-tni-i-i, Velo girl-e-e-e, white sleeves....”
The second part of the evening began... After midnight, we dispersed.

Goodbye, Bay Ganyo! Travel around Europe, carry to all corners the product of our beautiful Rose Valley, and... please, Bay Ganyo, look a little more deeply into European life, so that you may see its face, if only that cursed backwardness has not kept forcing itself upon you!...
